analysis.one_liner: Requires internet providers to treat all web traffic equally, without blocking or charging websites.
analysis.headline: The Senate's first net neutrality bill won 13 Democratic cosponsors but died in committee without a hearing or vote; no net neutrality statute was passed in the 109th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written 'net neutrality' rules into law: broadband providers like cable and phone companies could not block, slow down, or charge extra for access to any lawful website or service. It barred companies from forcing customers to buy bundled phone or cable TV service to get internet, and created a process for consumers to complain to the Federal Communications Commission, with the FCC required to resolve complaints within 90 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday internet users, small websites, and startups. The rules would guarantee that internet providers could not pick winners and losers online — for example, by slowing a streaming video service that competes with their own product, or charging a website a fee to reach customers at full speed. Small businesses and consumers without bargaining power would benefit most, since large companies can often pay for preferential treatment but individuals and small sites cannot.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits broadband providers from blocking, interfering with, discriminating against, or degrading any person's ability to use lawful content, applications, or services online.
Requires that content be treated on a reasonable and nondiscriminatory basis as to quality of service, access, speed, and bandwidth, and bans charges based on content type.
Stops providers from forcing subscribers to buy cable, telephone, or voice service as a condition of getting broadband.
Creates an FCC complaint process that must resolve net neutrality complaints within 90 days, with authority to order damages.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers — cable, telephone, and wireless companies. They could no longer sell prioritized 'fast lanes' to websites, collect fees from content companies to avoid being throttled, or force customers into expensive bundles.

drawbacks.text: Network management is genuinely complex: the bill allows reasonable management, but critics argue bright-line rules can make it harder to fight spam, congestion, and security threats. The bill does carve out security, parental controls, and non-discriminatory management, which blunts but does not eliminate this objection.

If providers cannot charge websites for faster delivery, they may recoup revenue through higher subscription prices or by building out less capacity, though the bill allows pricing tiers based on bandwidth and data volume sold to users.
The 'affiliated' definition includes companies with contract arrangements for distribution, raising the risk of litigation over what counts as discriminatory treatment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — an internet where providers cannot pick winners and losers — is large and broadly shared, and the bill's carve-outs for security and network management are sensible. The main costs fall on a concentrated industry that would lose an emerging revenue stream, and some compliance ambiguity might invite litigation. On balance, the bill was designed to preserve the open internet that enabled small businesses and free expression online.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never considered it; it died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 19, 2006 by Senator Olympia Snowe with six original cosponsors including Dorgan, Wyden, and Obama.
Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction; no further action was taken.
The bill attracted 13 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007 without the bill receiving a hearing or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers won: with no law on the books, they retained the ability to manage traffic and charge for prioritized service. Consumers and small websites gained nothing, and the fight moved to the FCC, whose authority was later contested and struck down in court before being partially reinstated in 2015 (and reversed again in 2017).

for.name: Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited six original cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: Byron Dorgan
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the net neutrality bill.

for.name: 13 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a bipartisan sponsor but no Republican cosponsor beyond Snowe.

against.name: Ted Stevens
against.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat without action until the Congress ended.

against.name: Cable and telephone broadband providers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against net neutrality legislation, arguing network management flexibility was needed and that mandates would discourage infrastructure investment.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 13 cosponsors were all Democrats plus its single Republican sponsor, and the Republican committee chairman never brought it up — a mostly party-line split with a notable bipartisan sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from selling fast-lane prioritization to websites or charging content companies for access, and would end forced bundling of phone or cable TV with internet service. Their gain in keeping those options open comes directly at the expense of an open internet for subscribers.
They could not be outbid by larger companies for faster delivery to customers, preserving the open internet on which they launch and compete.
Video, search, and social media companies would not have to pay broadband providers for guaranteed delivery speeds, keeping distribution costs low and universal.
